subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Why does sodium have a much lower melting point than aluminium in Period 3?
options: Aluminium has weaker metallic bonding due to its larger ions
Sodium is a giant covalent structure
Aluminium delocalises three electrons per atom and has a higher charge density, giving stronger metallic bonding
questions.explain: Al3+ has a smaller ion and contributes three delocalised electrons, so its metallic bonding is much stronger than that of Na, raising the melting point.

questions.q: A solution of [V(H2O)6]2+ is violet. The colour we see is:
options: The complementary colour of the wavelength absorbed
questions.explain: The transmitted/observed colour is complementary to the wavelengths of visible light that the complex absorbs.

questions.q: Which Period 3 oxide gives the most acidic solution when added to water?
questions.explain: SO3 reacts with water to form sulfuric acid, a strong acid, giving the lowest pH of the Period 3 oxides.

questions.q: Which species is responsible for the deep blue colour formed when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?
questions.explain: Ammonia partially substitutes water to give the deep blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ ion.

questions.q: Why are most aqueous transition-metal ions coloured?
options: Electrons are promoted between split d-orbitals, absorbing certain wavelengths of visible light
s-electrons are excited to higher p-orbitals
The metals emit light by nuclear decay
questions.explain: Ligands split the d-orbitals; absorption of visible light promotes a d-electron, and the complementary colour is transmitted.

questions.q: Why is [CuCl4]2- tetrahedral whereas [Cu(H2O)6]2+ is octahedral?
options: Chloride ions are larger and fewer can fit around the central ion
questions.explain: The larger chloride ligands mean only four can coordinate, giving a coordination number of 4 and a tetrahedral shape.

questions.q: What is meant by autocatalysis in the reaction between manganate(VII) and ethanedioate?
options: A product, Mn2+, catalyses the reaction so the rate increases as it proceeds
questions.explain: Mn2+ is a product that catalyses the reaction, so the rate increases once some Mn2+ has formed.

questions.q: When magnesium burns in oxygen, what is the product and the nature of its oxide?
questions.explain: Magnesium burns to form magnesium oxide, MgO, which is a basic (metal) oxide.

questions.q: What is the coordination number and shape of a complex ion with six monodentate ligands such as [Fe(H2O)6]2+?
questions.explain: Six monodentate ligands each donate one lone pair, giving coordination number 6 and an octahedral shape.

questions.q: What type of ligand is the ethanedioate (oxalate) ion, C2O4 2-?
questions.explain: Ethanedioate donates two lone pairs from two oxygen atoms, making it a bidentate ligand.

questions.q: Why is MgO only slightly soluble and weakly alkaline in water compared with Na2O?
options: Mg2+ has a higher charge density and MgO has stronger ionic bonding, limiting its reaction with water
MgO does not contain oxide ions
questions.explain: The stronger lattice and higher charge density of Mg2+ make MgO sparingly soluble, giving only a weakly alkaline suspension (about pH 9-10).

questions.q: Why is acidified barium chloride solution used to test for sulfate ions, and why is magnesium hydroxide used in medicine?
options: BaSO4 forms a white precipitate as it is insoluble; Mg(OH)2 is a sparingly soluble base used as an antacid
BaSO4 is green; Mg(OH)2 is a strong oxidiser
Both compounds are soluble and coloured
BaSO4 is soluble; Mg(OH)2 is a strong acid
questions.explain: The insolubility of BaSO4 gives a white precipitate confirming sulfate, while sparingly soluble Mg(OH)2 neutralises stomach acid as 'milk of magnesia'.

questions.q: Which factor would change the colour (wavelength absorbed) of a transition-metal complex?
options: Changing the volume of solvent only
questions.explain: Different ligands cause different d-orbital splitting energies, altering the wavelength absorbed and hence the observed colour.

questions.q: Why does the melting point fall sharply between silicon and phosphorus in Period 3?
options: Phosphorus has stronger covalent bonds than silicon
Phosphorus is a metal and silicon is not
The structure changes from giant covalent (Si) to simple molecular (P4), so only weak van der Waals forces are broken on melting phosphorus
questions.explain: Silicon's giant covalent lattice requires breaking many strong bonds, whereas molecular P4 needs only weak London forces overcome, giving a sharp drop.

questions.q: Silicon dioxide, SiO2, when classified by its acid-base behaviour is best described as:
options: An amphoteric oxide that dissolves in acid
An acidic oxide that is insoluble in water but reacts with hot concentrated alkali
questions.explain: SiO2 is acidic, reacting with hot concentrated NaOH to form a silicate, though it is insoluble in water.

questions.q: How does the oxidising ability of the halogens change down Group 7?
questions.explain: Oxidising ability decreases down Group 7 because larger atoms gain an electron less readily, so chlorine is a stronger oxidant than iodine.

questions.q: Which definition best describes a transition metal?
options: A metal that forms only +2 ions
A metal with a full d-subshell
A d-block metal that forms at least one stable ion with a partially filled d-subshell
questions.explain: Sc and Zn are excluded because their stable ions (Sc3+, Zn2+) have empty or full d-subshells, respectively.

questions.q: Aluminium oxide, Al2O3, is classified as amphoteric because it:
options: Reacts with both acids and bases
questions.explain: Al2O3 reacts with acids (forming Al3+ salts) and with alkalis (forming aluminate), so it is amphoteric.

questions.q: Why does scandium not behave as a typical transition metal?
options: Its only stable ion Sc3+ has an empty d-subshell
questions.explain: Sc3+ has the configuration [Ar] with no d-electrons, so it lacks the partially filled d-subshell needed for characteristic transition-metal behaviour.

questions.q: What is observed when sodium oxide, Na2O, is added to water?
options: It dissolves to give a strongly alkaline solution of NaOH
questions.explain: Na2O reacts vigorously with water to form sodium hydroxide, giving a solution of around pH 13-14.

questions.q: When NaOH(aq) is added to Al3+(aq) and then in excess, the observation is:
options: A blue precipitate that dissolves to deep blue
A white precipitate that dissolves in excess to a colourless solution
questions.explain: Al(OH)3 is amphoteric; it forms a white precipitate that redissolves in excess NaOH as [Al(OH)4]-.

questions.q: The relationship between the energy gap and the frequency of light absorbed by a complex is given by:
questions.explain: The d-orbital splitting energy equals Planck's constant times the frequency of the absorbed light, dE = h x frequency.

questions.q: Why is a small amount of chlorine added to drinking water despite its toxicity?
options: Its benefit in killing harmful microorganisms outweighs the risk of toxic effects
To increase the pH of the water
questions.explain: Chlorine kills pathogenic bacteria, so the public-health benefit is judged to outweigh the toxic risks.

questions.q: When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium iodide, why are products such as H2S and I2 formed?
options: Iodide ions are strong enough reducing agents to reduce sulfur from +6 to -2
The reaction is a simple neutralisation
Sulfuric acid acts only as an acid
questions.explain: Iodide is a powerful reducing agent and reduces sulfur in H2SO4 all the way to H2S (and gives I2), unlike chloride which only gives HCl.

questions.q: Why are manganate(VII) titrations self-indicating?
options: The Mn2+ product is intensely coloured
The purple MnO4- is decolourised, and the first excess drop turns the solution pink
questions.explain: MnO4- is decolourised as it reacts; the endpoint is the first permanent pale pink from a slight excess of MnO4-.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point of the halogens increase down Group 7?
options: Hydrogen bonding increases down the group
Metallic bonding develops down the group
Covalent bonds within molecules get stronger
Molecules get larger with more electrons, so London (van der Waals) forces between molecules increase
questions.explain: Larger halogen molecules have more electrons and stronger London forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the increasing reducing power of the halide ions?
questions.explain: Reducing power increases down the group as the larger ions lose their outer electron more readily, so I- is the strongest reducing agent.

questions.q: Why is barium more reactive than calcium toward water?
options: Barium's outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, so they are lost more easily, making it more reactive
Calcium has a larger atomic radius than barium
Barium has fewer protons than calcium
Barium has a higher first ionisation energy so reacts faster
questions.explain: Down Group 2 the outer electrons are further out and more shielded, lowering ionisation energy, so barium loses electrons (and reacts) more readily than calcium.

questions.q: Adding a few drops of NaOH(aq) to Fe2+(aq) produces:
questions.explain: Fe2+ gives a green precipitate of Fe(OH)2, which darkens to brown on standing as it oxidises to Fe(OH)3.

questions.q: The reaction between iodide and peroxodisulfate is catalysed by Fe2+/Fe3+ because:
options: Both reactants are negative and repel; Fe ions provide an alternative route with opposite-charge steps
questions.explain: S2O8 2- and I- are both negatively charged and repel; Fe ions act as an intermediate, alternating oxidation state to lower the activation energy.
